title: What would you monitor to prove your architecture is healthy?
description: Learn to define meaningful health signals, distinguish symptoms from root causes, and explain which metrics actually prove an architecture is working as intended.

data.text: Health is not the same as uptime. A system can be up but unhealthy if latency is climbing, errors are spiking, or queues are backing up. Good monitoring tells you whether the architecture is meeting its reliability and performance goals.
Google's Site Reliability Engineering book defines four signals that cover most user-facing failures.

items: Latency—how long requests take, split into successful and failed requests
Traffic—how much demand is being placed on your system
Errors—the rate of requests that fail
Saturation—how full your service is, typically measured by resource utilization such as CPU, memory, or queue depth

rows: Find broken dependencies or bad deploys
Spot slow dependencies or resource contention
Thread pools, connection pools, disk I/O

data.title: Health vs. uptime
data.text: Uptime measures whether the server responds. Health measures whether the system delivers value. A service can be up but unhealthy if it returns slow responses, corrupted data, or empty search results.

data.title: Alerting on symptoms, not causes
data.content: Instead of alerting on 'CPU > 90%', alert on 'p99 latency > 2 seconds AND error rate > 1%'. The symptom tells you users are affected; the cause may be CPU, lock contention, a slow dependency, or garbage collection.

data.title: Key takeaway
points: Monitor the four golden signals for every service
Use RED for request paths and USE for infrastructure
Alert on user-impacting symptoms, not just resource utilization
